newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-FRENCH SET FOR FIVE NATIONS CORONATION.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FRENCH SET FOR FIVE NATIONS CORONATION.

text.p: France will be crowned as the new kings of European rugby this month unless Scotland can spoil what looks like a pre-destined Five Nations script at Parc des Princes in a fortnight.

The French have collected the title in 1967, 1977 and 1987 and, barring a complete disaster in Paris, will extend that remarkable sequence after a 23-20 victory over England which left Twickenham in a state of shock on Saturday.
There was barely a soul in the 75,000 crowd who believed it possible that England could squander a 20-6 lead going into the final quarter.

They managed it somehow, allowing a French side who had spent the first hour running into a brick wall to emerge battered and bruised with their first win on English soil for a decade and a potential grand slam ahead of them.

"If England had won we couldn't have complained, but we kept going," said assistant coach Pierre Villepreux, reflecting on an extraordinary finale which brought converted tries for Laurent Leflamand and Christophe Lamaison, followed by Lamaison's winning penalty with four minutes left.

"In the end our philosophy won it," added Villepreux, the former international turned coaching guru who has only recently been welcomed back into the French set-up. "We played the rugby I like and we played it well. Mentally we were superior."
England coach Jack Rowell, who described what unfolded as "the worst 20 minutes of my life", had seen his team play a praiseworthy game for an hour in windy conditions.

Lawrence Dallaglio appeared to have put his side on their way to a third consecutive title with a try a minute before half-time and fly-half Paul Grayson kicked four penalties and a drop-goal to underline England's forward domination.

Had he not missed one of the easiest kicks of his career from in front of the posts after half an hour, it might have been a totally different story. Instead, France dug in mightily and found in Lamaison a man totally unruffled by the big occasion.

The Brive centre scored 70 points to assist his club to the European club title earlier this season and his 18 points, including a well-taken try, two conversions, two penalties and a drop-goal, established a new personal French record in the fixture, beating Guy Laporte's 17 points in 1986.
"We always had confidence in him as a goalkicker," said coach Jean-Claude Skrela. "He was a leading character in our win today but the whole team deserves praise."

Any side who can restrict England, rampant in the closing stages against Scotland and Ireland, to just one kickable penalty in the second half deserves credit, particularly with the loss of inspirational captain Abdel Benazzi with 15 minutes left.
But this was a match England held in the palm of their hands and a triple crown should they beat Wales in Cardiff will be scant consolation.
"You expect to build on a 20-6 lead not lose it," said Rowell. "Perhaps we thought the game was over. We won't make the same mistake again."

Rowell played down earlier hints he is to quit the England job because of his business commitments, but may find time to ponder on the trials and tribulations of his former Bath colleague Brian Ashton.
Ashton was handed a six-year contract as coach of Ireland this week, only to see his new side suffer a second record defeat in as many matches en route to a probable wooden spoon.

The Irish crashed 38-10 to Scotland, who profited from the return of former rugby league man Alan Tait after a nine-year test absence, leaving Ashton to deny his side were now a second division rugby nation.
"There's no excuse for this performance but we're still in the first division," he said. "There's no relegation from the Five Nations."
